Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

when we turned off the lights and checked that the upper window was shut", "output": "We opened the repair cafe in the old library meeting room on the second Saturday of April because the community hall roof was being checked and we could not use the usual tables. The room has a side entrance, a low sink, and a narrow cupboard where the library kept folding chairs. Our sign was taped to the glass, and the first visitors came in before we had finished setting up. Nobody seemed bothered by the boxes in the aisle, but we moved them before anyone brought in a heavy appliance.

The welcome table is going to be beside the sink so visitors can wash their hands before they handle a donated object and keep the entrance clear. We borrowed two green cloths from the library and used one to cover the table. The other cloth stayed folded near the kettle because we were not sure whether the sink would be needed for rinsing parts. Mara took names and wrote down what each person hoped to repair. She asked visitors to describe the problem rather than promising that every item could be fixed. A man brought a radio that hummed but gave no sound, and a child arrived with a wooden toy whose wheel had come loose.

We agreed on the room plan while the kettle warmed. The extension lead ran along the wall and was covered with a rubber cable ramp. The volunteer who watched the doorway asked people not to step over the lead, even though it looked flat. We put the first aid kit on the cupboard shelf and the fire exit map beside the light switch. The back window would stay unlocked during the session, but we kept the door itself closed because the latch had caught the previous week. The room was busy and warm, so we opened the upper window for air and checked that nobody had left a bag beneath it. One of the library staff said, “Please leave the chairs in a clear line along the far wall because a reading group needs them on Monday.” We did that and left a gap beside the cupboard for the folding trolley.

Our volunteers had different levels of experience, and we made that clear on the sign at the entrance. The electrical bench was for items that could be unplugged before inspection, and anything with a damaged power cord went into a red tray until a qualified volunteer could look at it. Nobody was asked to open a sealed battery pack. Jo checked small kitchen appliances while Priya handled lamps and desk fans. There were safety glasses for visitors who wanted to watch, but children had to stay with an adult and away from the soldering station. Priya will lead the soldering bench because Jon has to leave before lunch to collect his mother. The soldering station stayed on the far table with a heatproof mat and a metal stand for the iron. Jon still helped sort screws into jars and showed two new volunteers how to test a switch without touching bare wire. We kept spare fuses in labeled drawers rather than putting loose ones on the table.

The first repair was a desk lamp with a cracked plug casing. The owner said it had been flickering for weeks and then stopped after she moved it to another room. Priya saw that the cord insulation was split near the plug and did not connect it to the test socket. She explained that the cafe could replace the plug if the cord itself was still sound, but this cord had to be replaced too. The owner agreed to leave the lamp for a closer inspection and wrote her phone number on the repair card. The radio made a low hum when Jo checked it, and its speaker wire had slipped from a small connector. He reattached the wire and tested the radio at low volume before giving it back. The visitor stayed beside him and said, “My father used to listen to the weather on this every morning, so I am glad it is making a sound again.” The wooden toy took longer because the loose wheel had worn its wooden peg thin. We did not glue it immediately. We showed the child and her grandmother the worn part and asked whether they wanted us to fit a new peg. The grandmother said yes and kept the old wheel in a paper envelope.

At midday we stopped repairs for a short safety check and counted the items waiting on the shelf. The count was seven, not six, and we wrote that number on the board so the afternoon volunteers could compare it with the cards. We made a list for the next session:
1. Ask the library whether we can borrow their small vice again.
2. Bring another rubber cable ramp because the spare one has a split edge.
3. Call the lamp owner after testing the replacement cord.
4. Keep the radio repair card until Jo has added the name of the connector he used.
5. Check with the caretaker about the window latch before the next cafe.

The list was read aloud, and one volunteer pointed out that the vice belonged to the tool club, not the library, so we wrote “tool club” on the note rather than sending the question to the wrong person. The split ramp was placed in a box marked “Do not use,” and nobody took it back to the floor.

After lunch two visitors came in with a hand mixer that smelled hot and a small fan that rattled when it turned. We unplugged the mixer and left it on the inspection tray because the owner could not remember whether it had been used after the smell started. The fan had a loose grille screw and a buildup of dust around the guard. The volunteer removed the grille with the owner watching and cleaned the dust with a soft brush. The blades turned freely afterward, but we asked the owner to try it at home while standing nearby and to bring it back if the rattle returned. We did not use compressed air because it could have pushed dust into the motor. A teenager helped sort the donated screws by length and found three that fit the fan grille. We kept the other screws in separate jars rather than guessing where they belonged.

We had planned to pack away at three, but the caretaker said the room was booked until half past three for a language class, so we kept the tool tables in place and moved the finished items to the windowsill. Each owner checked their own card before leaving, and the radio owner signed that he had collected it. The lamp remained in the cupboard because the replacement cord had not arrived. The hand mixer stayed in the red tray, and its owner took a card with the cafe contact details. If the cupboard still smells damp on Friday, we will leave its door open and ask the library staff to check the pipe behind it before putting tools away there again. The caretaker showed us a small water mark low on the wall but did not know when it had appeared, so we wrote the date beside it and told the library contact what we had seen.

Before we locked up, we counted the chairs and returned the trolley to the side entrance. The first aid kit was still on the shelf, and the exit map had not been covered by the sign. We wiped the table near the sink and left the second green cloth folded where the library staff could find it. Mara put the repair cards in an envelope for the next session, and the volunteers took home only their own labeled tools. We wrote down that the cafe had repaired the radio and toy while the lamp and mixer still needed follow-up. The room was quieter by then, and the caretaker asked us to use the side entrance when we came back the following month. We thanked her and made a note to bring fresh tape for the glass sign because one corner had started to peel during the afternoon. The last visitor had already gone when we turned off the lights and checked that the upper window was shut."}]
